image5.jpg.alt: Cross-section of airspace classes A, B, C, D, E, and G.
image5.jpg.description: The diagram places Class A above 18,000 feet MSL, with its upper boundary labeled FL600. Class B is drawn as stacked shelves around a large airport, Class C as two shelves, and Class D as a smaller surface column. Class E fills much of the controlled airspace between these areas. Class G is shown near the ground where controlled airspace does not extend to the surface. This is a schematic teaching diagram, not a chart for determining airspace at a real location.

image19.png.alt: Sectional-chart training example showing terrain, airports, and overlapping airspace boundaries.
image19.png.description: This dense chart excerpt illustrates why a pilot must examine boundary colors and line styles, airport symbols, altitude labels, and terrain together. Use the chart workflow in the preceding text and the airspace comparison table in section 2.9. Open the original figure to magnify individual labels; this historical illustration is not a current navigation chart.

image13.jpg.alt: Airport diagram comparing left-hand and right-hand traffic patterns.
image13.jpg.description: The pattern legs are departure, crosswind, downwind, base, and final. Two rectangular circuits illustrate turns on opposite sides of a runway. A segmented circle, traffic-pattern indicators, landing-direction indicator, wind cone, and landing runway indicators are also shown. The marked no-transgression zones are beside the runway ends. Read the surrounding airport-operations text for the role of these indicators.

image11.jpg.alt: Illustrated Runway 23 threshold, centerline, edge markings, and adjacent taxiway.
image11.jpg.description: The runway illustration labels the threshold with the number 23. White threshold stripes, a dashed white centerline, and white runway edge lines distinguish the runway from the adjacent taxiway, which uses yellow markings. The preceding text explains runway numbering and reciprocal directions.

image9.jpg.alt: A crewed aircraft approaching nearly head-on over mountainous terrain.
image9.jpg.description: The view illustrates the need to detect an approaching aircraft and yield. The accompanying text explains that an aircraft with little apparent relative movement that grows larger can be on a collision course.

image18.jpg.alt: An analog aircraft altimeter with a numbered dial and multiple hands.
image18.jpg.description: This instrument illustrates pressure-based altitude measurement. The surrounding section explains atmospheric pressure, altimeter settings, and the distinction between pressure readings and altitude references.

image6.jpg.alt: Diagram of rising thermals over a plowed field, marsh, and town, drifting with the wind.
image6.jpg.description: Sun-heated ground warms adjacent air, which rises in thermal columns and can form cumulus clouds near the condensation level. The illustration contrasts good thermal sources over a plowed field and town with a moist marsh that produces weaker thermals, and shows the columns drifting downwind.

image2.jpg.alt: A red-and-white windsock extended beside an airfield.
image2.jpg.description: A windsock gives a visual indication of surface wind direction and approximate strength. The nearby text distinguishes ordinary wind changes from wind shear and its hazards near the surface.

image8.jpg.alt: Fog filling a mountain valley beneath clearer air and higher ridges.
image8.jpg.description: The photograph illustrates a valley inversion: stable air can limit vertical mixing and trap fog, smoke, haze, or pollutants in low terrain. The temperature-inversion paragraph and stable-versus-unstable-air table provide the textual explanation.

image3.jpg.alt: National Weather Service cloud chart grouping photographs by cloud-base height and cloud form.
image3.jpg.description: The chart groups high clouds with bases roughly 16,000–50,000 feet, middle clouds roughly 6,500–23,000 feet, and low clouds from the surface to roughly 6,500 feet. High types include cirrus, cirrostratus, and cirrocumulus; middle types include altostratus and altocumulus; low types include stratus, stratocumulus, cumulus, and cumulonimbus. Photographs compare thin wisps, sheets and layers, rounded cloud elements, and strong vertical development. The surrounding text explains the operational significance of cloud form and stability.

image12.jpg.alt: Layered, flattened cloud bands above an open landscape.
image12.jpg.description: The textbook uses this photograph as a lenticular-cloud example. Lenticular clouds can be associated with strong winds and mountain-wave conditions; the instructional point is to consider wind and turbulence rather than treating smooth-looking clouds as proof of calm air.

image7.jpg.alt: Cumulus clouds with vertically growing towers above a landscape.
image7.jpg.description: The photograph shows rounded cloud towers extending upward. It illustrates the preceding explanation that increasing vertical cloud development can signal strengthening convection.

image4.jpg.alt: Diagram of the cumulus, mature, and dissipating stages of a thunderstorm.
image4.jpg.description: In the cumulus stage, rising air builds the cloud. The mature stage combines updrafts and downdrafts with precipitation, lightning, and a spreading anvil. The dissipating stage is dominated by descending air. The adjacent three-row table supplies the stage characteristics in text.

image15.jpg.alt: A layer of fog around buildings at dawn or dusk.
image15.jpg.description: This photograph accompanies the textbook’s comparison of radiation, advection, and upslope fog. The nearby table gives each fog type’s formation process and typical clues; the photograph alone does not establish a specific fog type.

image17.jpg.alt: Vehicles and roadside trees becoming difficult to see through dense fog.
image17.jpg.description: The photograph illustrates how fog reduces visibility. The source caption discusses steam fog, while the surrounding fog table explains different formation mechanisms. The photograph alone is not used to identify the mechanism.

image16.jpg.alt: Automated airport weather instruments mounted on a platform and mast.
image16.jpg.description: The station photograph illustrates ASOS/AWOS surface observations. The nearby text explains that the measurements describe conditions at the station, which may differ from conditions at a UAS operating site.

image1.jpg.alt: Annotated METAR with eleven labeled groups; the complete report and explanation follow in text.
image1.jpg.transcript: METAR KBNA 281251Z AUTO 12008KT 4SM -RA HZ BKN010 OVC023 21/17 A3005 RMK RAB25
image1.jpg.description: The labeled groups are report type, station, observation time, automated-source modifier, wind, visibility, weather, sky condition, temperature/dew point, altimeter setting, and remarks. KBNA identifies Nashville. The observation is for the 28th at 1251 UTC. Wind is from 120 degrees at 8 knots; visibility is 4 statute miles, with light rain and haze. Broken cloud is reported at 1,000 feet and overcast at 2,300 feet. Temperature is 21°C and dew point 17°C. The altimeter setting is 30.05 inches Hg. The rain-began remark indicates 25 minutes past the hour, or 1225 UTC in this example.

image10.jpg.alt: Annotated South Bend TAF training example; the report text and interpretation follow.
image10.jpg.transcript:
TAF KSBN 171145Z 171212 VRB03KT 2 SM SCT030 BKN080 TEMPO 1517 SHRA
FM2200 13009KT 1SM OVC030 BECMG0210 NSW BKN030
image10.jpg.description: The supplied slide identifies South Bend, an issue time on the 17th at 1145 UTC, and a validity period from 1200 to 1200. It describes variable wind at 3 knots, 2 statute miles visibility, scattered clouds at 3,000 feet, and broken clouds at 8,000 feet, with temporary rain showers from 1500 to 1700. From 2200 it gives wind from 130 degrees at 9 knots, 1 statute mile visibility, and overcast at 3,000 feet. Its final explanation gives no significant weather and broken clouds at 3,000 feet between 0200 and 1000. This is the historical training example as supplied, not a current forecast.
